chunks: Ibn Mahboub, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Ammar al-Sabati, from Abu Ubeyda, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a blind man who deliberately blinded the eye of a healthy person. He (peace be upon him) said: 'O Abu Ubeyda! The deliberation of the blind man is like the error. In this case, the wergild (diyah) is from his own wealth. So if he does not have wealth, then his wergild is upon the Imam, and the right of a Muslim is not invalidated.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on compensation for a blind person who causes injury?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Baqir (AS) clarifies that a blind person’s intentional injury is legally treated as error (*khata’*), with compensation drawn from their personal wealth or, if insolvent, from the Imam’s treasury (*bayt al-mal*). This ruling underscores the Shia principle of *la yabtilu haqq muslim* (no Muslim’s right is nullified), ensuring that physical disability does not diminish one’s financial liability or the victim’s entitlement to *diyah*. The narration highlights the practical application of equitable justice in Islamic jurisprudence, where the state acts as a guarantor of rights when individual capacity is lacking.

en.hubeali: Ibn Mahboub, from Hisham Bin Salim, from Ammar Al Sabaty, from Abu Ubeyda who said,

‘I asked Abu Ja’far<sup>asws</sup> about a blind (man) who blinded an eye of a correct one deliberately. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘O Abu Ubeyda! The deliberation of the blind is like the error. In this in the wergild from his own wealth. So if there does not happen to be wealth for him, so his wergild is upon the Imam<sup>asws</sup>, and a right of a Muslim would not be invalidated’.
